title: Adaptive speculative decoding: picking draft lengths at runtime
gist: A provider's simulation study. A policy re-chooses the draft length at every scheduler step from the live batch size, an estimate of how many guesses are accepted, and a cost model of the engine. Acceptance was measured on a real model; throughput and latency come from an open-source simulator of a vLLM-shaped engine. The policy matches the best fixed draft length chosen in hindsight at every load.
changes: At a steady load, adaptive speculation only ties a well-chosen fixed setting; its value is never being badly wrong when the load moves. The simulator is a second kind of measuring rig, pricing an idea before it is built. C4 named that as what would weaken it. Nobody has checked it against a real engine.
caveats: Only acceptance is measured. Engine and chip costs are modelled, and the simulator's notes call its figures upper bounds for a perfect engine. One model, one workload, decode only. No speed-up of adaptive over fixed is given. The author expects it to be hard to build. The remark that coding agents are poor at finding engine settings is asserted, not shown.

bears_on.note: The best draft length moves with the batch size, and which of two drafters is cheaper to run flips with it.
A simulator is the cheap oracle this claim says would weaken it, but only acceptance is measured and it has not been compared with a real engine.
